issues.title: CCA attester model
issues.author: thomas-fossati
issues.body:
The CCA attester model is slightly more complicated than is currently described.

There are _two_ separate sub-attesters (platform and realm) rather than one, each with their independent AE/TE split, and bound via RAK attestation.

This should be explained in Section 3 and illustrated in Figure 1.

issues.title: In delegated mode, should `eat_nonce` be `rak_pub_hash_value` instead?
issues.author: thomas-fossati
issues.body:
There is potential semantic ambiguity in using `eat_nonce` for the binder in delegated mode.

In particular,

1. it's not a proper challenge issued by the ABI caller
2. freshness properties associated with the claim are not clear.

It seems easier to create a new claim with explicit semantics, e.g., `rak_pub_hash_value`.

comments.author: SimonFrost-Arm
comments.body: Would better documentation for the usage of eat_nonce in this profile suffice? My concern about adding an explicit binder for delegate is ambiguity on presence or not of eat_nonce in the same platform report: should they both be there / what are there relation / if no eat_nonce then will profile implementers be confident of freshness?  Keeping eat_nonce allows re-use of the platform report in multiple layerings, including both binding and as a pure freshness challenge.

comments.author: gmandyam

I think the use of eat-nonce is consistent with https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9334#name-implicit-timekeeping-using-.  

This is because in this case the eat-nonce provides an implicit indication of time, namely the time at which the RAK was generated and bound to the platform token.

issues.title: algorithm ID claim string is discouraged?
issues.author: deeglaze
issues.body:
I'm reviewing the attestation design for our ARM silicon and I see

> The CCA platform hash algorithm ID claim is a text string that identifies the algorithm used to calculate the extended measurements in the CCA platform token.
> The string SHOULD be encoded according to "Hash Name String" in the "Named Information Hash Algorithm Registry" [IANA.named-information].

My understanding from Henk is that the text is discouraged and the number in [[IANA.named-information](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ffm-rats-cca-token-00.html#IANA.named-information)] is preferred. I'd like the text to allow for both with `text / int` and say

The CCA platform hash algorithm ID claim is a text string or integer that identifies the algorithm used to calculate the extended measurements int the CCA platform token.
> If the identifier is an integer, it MUST denote to the corresponding algorithm in the IANA.named-information hash algorithm registry.
> If the identifier is a string, it SHOULD be encoded according to "Hash Name String" in the "Named Information Hash Algorithm Registry" [IANA.named-information].


Similar for `cca-realm-hash-algo-id-label`, `cca-realm-public-key-hash-algo-id-label`.

comments.author: SimonFrost-Arm
comments.body: I'll review, but background is that pinning down a standard naming that corresponds to an IANA registry proved difficult. The named hash algo was a recommendation from IANA expert review. RFC6920, which established that registry, is text based and notes that the numeric ID is optional. Do you have a ref for the deprecation? We'll need a stable ref & usage for further IANA registration of evidence claims.

comments.author: thomas-fossati
comments.body:
> Do you have a ref for the deprecation?

I am not aware of any plans to deprecate the textual version in favor of its numeric counterpart.

The reason ID is optional is that the codepoint space is severely limited, with only 63 possible IDs, of which 12 are already allocated.

If the registry wants to have any chance of long-term survival, it **must** allow text.

I am unsure why this decision was made initially; it seems quite short-sighted, but we can't (easily) change that.

issues.title: Clarification needed: exact input bytes for the platform challenge (token binding) hash
issues.author: Ruach
issues.body:
Problem Statement

The CCA token specification defines the platform challenge as a hash of the Realm Attestation Key (RAK), used to bind the platform and realm tokens. However, the spec does not state what byte representation of the RAK should be used as the hash input.

```
cca-hash-type = bytes .size 32 / bytes .size 48 / bytes .size 64
cca-platform-challenge-label = 10
cca-platform-challenge = (
    cca-platform-challenge-label => cca-hash-type
)
```
What should be the correct input to be hashed?

Raw uncompressed EC point: 0x04 || X || Y (97 bytes for P-384)
CBOR-encoded COSE_Key: a CBOR map as defined by COSE
Request
The spec should explicitly state which byte representation of the RAK MUST be used as the input to the hash function when computing the cca-platform-challenge binding value.

issues.title: Profile forbids Detached EAT Bundle, blocking standard binding of detached evidence (FAL, CMEM raw evidence / certificate chain and sub-attester)
issues.author: dkumar-nv
issues.body:
**Draft:** `draft-ffm-rats-cca-token-03`
## Summary
 
The reference profile pins both CMW entries to `application/eat+cwt` (CoAP Content-Format 263) and **explicitly prohibits** Detached EAT Bundles (`application/eat-bun+cbor`, CF 265). This removes the only EAT-standard mechanism (RFC 9711 §4.2.18.2 + §5) for cryptographically binding large detached claims sets to the signed CCA Platform token. Three concrete use cases are:
 
1. **Live Firmware Activation (LFA) Firmware Activity Log** — §4.6.1.2 requires it for measurement reconstruction but does not specify how it is conveyed.
2. **CMEM (and similar PDEV) raw SPDM evidence and certificate chain** — §4.6.5 carries only digests (keys `2` and `3` of `arm-platform-extension-device-common`); the underlying raw bytes have no specified transport.
3. **Composite attesters embedded as software components** — a software component listed in `arm-platform-sw-components` (e.g., a CPU complex composed of chiplets / accelerators, each with its own attesting environment) is itself a layered/composite attester and produces a sub-token. There is no mechanism to bind that sub-token to the Platform token.

Adding more entries to the top-level CMW Collection is not a viable workaround (the reasons are detailed in [§ Why the top-level CMW Collection is not a viable workaround](#why-the-top-level-cmw-collection-is-not-a-workaround)).
 
---
 
## Background
 
### What the draft currently mandates
 
§4.1 fixes the top-level CMW structure to a single content format:
 
```cddl
; CoAP Content-Format for "application/eat+cwt"
eat-cwt-coap-cf = 263
 
cca-token-cmw = {
  0xACCA => [ eat-cwt-coap-cf, bytes .cbor COSE_Sign1<arm-platform-claims> ],
  0xACD1 => [ eat-cwt-coap-cf, bytes .cbor COSE_Sign1<cca-realm-claims>   ]
}
```
 
The Baseline Profile (§4.11.3, Table 2) reinforces this with:
 
> **Detached EAT Bundle Usage** — Detached EAT bundles MUST NOT be sent
 
And §4.11.1 adds:
 
> The CCA Platform token is always directly signed by the CCA Platform RoT. Therefore, the CCA Platform claims-set is never carried in a Detached EAT bundle.
 
### EAT standard mechanisms (RFC 9711)
 
RFC 9711 §4.2.18 defines three submodule types. Amongst them, Detached-Submodule-Digest is the only EAT-standard way to convey large or variable-size evidence externally while keeping it bound to the signed parent token. RFC 9782 §6.9 registers CF 265 specifically for this purpose.
 
---
 
## Concrete gaps
 
### Gap 1 — LFA Firmware Activity Log
 
§4.6.1.2 (Measurement Value) states:
 
> If the CCA platform supports Live Firmware Activation then the value reported in attestation may have been further extended by measurements of updates to the software component. In this case, the value of the measurement must be validated by reconstructing the reported value using information from the **Firmware Activity Log**.
 
The draft does not specify:
 
- a transport for the FAL;
- a label/identifier under which a verifier should look it up.
**Inlining** the FAL as a `Claims-Set` submodule is impractical because activity logs grow unbounded over the deployment lifetime of the platform. The EAT-standard fit is a `Detached-Submodule-Digest` entry (e.g., labelled `"fal"`) under the `submods` claim, with the full FAL Claims-Set conveyed alongside in a DEB.
 
### Gap 2 — CMEM raw SPDM evidence and certificate chain
 
`arm-platform-extension` currently encodes only digests of off-platform evidence:
 
```cddl
arm-platform-extension = (
    arm-platform-extension-label => [ + arm-platform-extension-device ]
)
arm-platform-extension-device = {
    arm-platform-extension-device-common
    (
        ( ; ---- VCA digest required ----
            5 => $protocols-support-vca,    ; protocol, e.g. "spdm-1.2.3"
            6 => arm-platform-hash-type,             ; SPDM VCA digest
        )
     // ( ; ---- no VCA needed ----
            5 => text                       ; protocol
        )
    )
    (
        (
            7 => $type-with-encryption,     ; device type, e.g. "cxl-type-3
            8 => &encryption-type,          ; indicates encryption type
        )
     // ( ; ---- no encryption type needed ----
            7 => text
        )
    )
}
arm-platform-extension-device-common = (
    ? 1 => text,                       ; hash algorithm identifier
      2 => arm-platform-hash-type,     ; device measurements exchange digest
      3 => arm-platform-hash-type,     ; certificate chain digest
      4 => bool,                       ; indicates whether this PDEV uses IDE
)
```
 
A remote verifier appraising a CMEM (or any PDEV) instance needs the raw underlying data, not just the digests. The draft does not specify how the raw SPDM exchanges or the certificate chain are transported.
 
### Gap 3 — Composite attesters embedded as software components
 
§3 explicitly scopes CCA to *"a 'layered attester' (Section 3.2 of [RFC9334]) with exactly two layers: platform and realm"*. However, the individual entries in `arm-platform-sw-components` (§4.6.1) can themselves be composite attesters. A CPU may have multiple chiplets, security co-processors, and on-package accelerators. Each such component (sub-attester) may have their own attesting environment and produce their own evidence (sub-token), which must roll up into the Platform token without losing provenance, signing key, or scope.
 
Three structural points follow:
 
1. The sub-token may have its **own signature** under the sub-attester's key. It cannot be re-signed by the Platform RoT without breaking the trust chain.
2. The sub-token may have its **own `submods`** namespace — its own DICE concise-evidence, its own measurement logs, its own further nested sub-attesters. This is recursion, not a flat list.
3. If the sub-token itself needs to convey detached claims sets (e.g., a long firmware activity log of the chiplet), it requires DEB *as a sub-token of the Platform token's DEB or CWT*.
The current draft has no way to represent composite attesters such as ones described above, and the top-level CMW Collection cannot rescue it (see next section).
 
---
 
## Why the top-level CMW Collection is not a viable workaround
 
### 1. CMW does not suffice for binding without re-implementing DEB semantics
 
Adding a claim such as FAL in CMW without cryptographically linking to the signed token will allow adversary to substitute the claim with another while evading detection. In order to fix this, a digest of such claim will need to be present in the signed token. But this amounts to re-implementing `Detached-Submodule-Digest` semantics ad-hoc, per need, without the standardized pattern that RFC 9711 already provides.
 
### 2. Flattening destroys hierarchical scoping (an OO-design / encapsulation violation)
 
Each token in the assembly has its own logical scope:
 
```
Top-level assembly
├── Platform Token (scope: platform RoT)
│   ├── submod: "fal"            (scope: platform's software components)
│   ├── submod: "cmem-1"          (scope: platform-attached PDEV #1)
│   ├── submod: "cmem-2"          (scope: platform-attached PDEV #2)
│   └── submod: "cpu-complex"     (scope: composite sub-attester)
│       ├── submod: "chiplet-a"   (scope: sub-attester's internal layer)
│       └── submod: "chiplet-b"   (scope: sub-attester's internal layer)
└── Realm Token (scope: realm RMM)
    └── submod: ...               (scope: realm guest measurements)
```
 
Promoting every leaf to the top-level CMW Collection collapses this tree:
 
```
Top-level CMW Collection (flat list, no scope)
├── Platform Token
├── Realm Token
├── FAL log                                  ← whose FAL?
├── CMEM-1 SPDM exchange                     ← which device?
├── CMEM-1 cert chain                        ← which chain belongs to which exchange?
├── CMEM-2 SPDM exchange
├── CMEM-2 cert chain
├── CPU-complex composite token
├── CPU-complex chiplet-a evidence           ← whose chiplet?
├── CPU-complex chiplet-b evidence
├── Realm guest evidence                     ← inside platform or realm scope?
└── ...
```
 
Every name now lives in a single global namespace. Two devices of the same type need distinct keys at the top level. The verifier loses the ability to ask "what are *this token's* submodules?" and must instead correlate by side-channel naming conventions. This is exactly the encapsulation violation that the `submods` claim is designed to prevent: a token's submodules live inside *that token*, not as peers of it.
 
### 3. Composite attesters (Gap 3) cannot be represented
 
The "promote to top level" workaround is structurally impractical for nested composite attesters. A sub-attester's evidence is itself a signed token with its own `submods` claim and its own further sub-attesters. Promoting that to the top-level CMW Collection would require also promoting *its* submodules to the top level and so on recursively thereby requiring the CMW creation task to require internal knowledge of the topology. The CMW creator will also need to ensure that it selects a unique name for CMW entry to avoid collisions. Lastly, the CMW profile will become per attester as the list of submods will vary depending upon the specific attester.
 
### 4. Verifier search complexity and execution time increases and policy may become fragile
 
With hierarchical `submods`, a verifier appraises a token by walking *its own submodules* — a local, scoped operation. With a flat top-level CMW Collection, the verifier must, for every entry, search the *entire* Collection to find related entries.

Verifier policy (CoRIM reference value matching, `authorized-by` checks, etc.) will likely need to encode "which top-level entry belongs to which parent" explicitly. This is fragile and can be avoided using standard submods with DEB.
 
### 5. Side-by-side comparison
 
| Concern | Flat top-level CMW expansion | DEB with `submods` (RFC 9711) |
|---|---|---|
| Cryptographic binding of detached data to parent token | ❌ None at the wrapper level | ✅ Digest in signed parent + DEB pairing |
| Naming scope | ❌ Single flat global namespace | ✅ Per-token, per-`submods` claim |
| Composite / layered attester support | ❌ Cannot represent recursion | ✅ Native (nested tokens, recursive submods) |
| Verifier search complexity | ❌ Global search and correlation | ✅ Local tree walk per token |
| Profile portability | ❌ CCA-specific layout conventions, CMW profile becomes attester specific | ✅ Same pattern across EAT profiles |
| Standard EAT mechanism | ❌ Re-invents Detached-Submodule-Digest ad-hoc forcing new verifier work | ✅ RFC 9711 implies no new verifier work |
 
---
 
## Proposed direction
Relax §4.1 and §4.11.3 so that the `0xACCA` entry MAY use either CF 263 (`eat+cwt`) or CF 265 (`eat-bun+cbor`). When CF 265 is used:
 
- the bundle's `main-token` remains the same `COSE_Sign1<arm-platform-claims>`, so signing flow and key material are unchanged;
- the `submods` claim (RFC 9711 §4.2.18, key 266) is added to `arm-platform-claims` with one entry per detached artifact (e.g., `"fal"`, `"cmem-1"`, `"cpu-complex"`), each carrying either a `Detached-Submodule-Digest` or a `Nested-Token` (CWT/DEB) as appropriate;
- the bundle's `detached-claims-sets` map carries the corresponding Claims-Sets under matching labels.

---

comments.body:
> DEB is an existing standardized method for binding while CMW one will force proprietary design. For avoidance of doubt: CMW is not proprietary nor would signing of CMW be but the usage will be 

As hopefully I'll expand below, the nature of the platform and relation to the other components in CCA attestation doesn't fit the simplified assumptions of DEB binding. 

> (and there will also be a matter of needing 2 keys which is not always available but I won't get into that unless necessary)

The CMW does not need to be signed. The basis of security is the signature of the PAT and other members of the collection have inter-component security bindings.


> A single CPU can still be a lead attester with one or more sub-attesters (chiplet-a and chiplet-b). 

To reiterate: the CCA platform is a single entity, capturing the boot state including the security lifecycle and the firmware executing in the CCA TCB per the SM. All APs must have the same boot state. Thus there is no need for different submods per chiplet/socket and we refer to the FAL as being the entity that describes the live journey for the platform. The extra evidence about other processing instances is only required if their RoTs can't guarantee a common (platform) hardware identity in which case the peer-signers concept allows those separate identities to be available.

> I think what would help a lot in understanding your thought process is a complete token + CMW for the following situation. Can you please provide?

Note given comment above, this part of the response doesn't match the breakdown requested, but describes a full set of CCA attestation components.

Beyond the platform above (PAT) there is one guaranteed additional set of workload claims: the realm token. These two can have different binding methods depending upon implementation so reside together better in a collection than in any EAT hierarchy.

There are then a set of optional evidence components. The likelihood of these existing varies from implementation to implementation. The data for many of these lives in the host so needs to be assembled at realm level to the token.
+ FAL  - present if implementation implements LFA.  Security lives in PAT and thus no other binding is required.
+ Comprehensive trust devices - CMEM devices are the key use cases here and hence the security bindings for these must live in the PAT. The bindings are held as an array and the host prepares a single CDAT for all the devices.
+ Selective trust devices - not all deployments may require this as the Realm code already has to validate and accept the device evidence. Binding values are within the RAT as the RMM stores them during device assignment interaction. Bindings are held as an array and the Realm can prepare a single SDAT for all the devices.
The process of verifying DAT data is consistent across SDAT and CDAT and has multiple phases: the items within the DAT are validated against their binding values / if the items are transcripts then the transcript validity is checked and the artifacts extracted / the artifacts are validated against RVs or Policy for trustworthiness.
+ Endorsements / RVs - not present in all deployments. Use case is that for a given deployment the host has more immediate access to these than the verifier. They are included in the collection as a convenience for the deployment. Examples: intermediate certs / CoRIM for workload measurements. There is no binding required for these as they are independently verifiable.

A lead verifier for CCA can examine the CMW map to determine which of the above components are present and then these can be validated by more specific sub-verifiers dedicated to the relevant formats. Binding checks between the components can either be provided by serial validation of dependent component or post verification across the (sub) attestation results.

> Can you explain how the above is different from adding a new component to array of sw-components? Can you also cite the specific scenario? For example: For case of lead attester, I don't see why ABI will be impacted

To add a new sw-component, the attester just adds another element to an existing structure. 
The scenario I was trying to capture was: to add a new DCS, it's necessary to add a new submodule in the main token, that contains a hash of the DCS. That hash needs to be computed over the DCS and passed to the producing component for the main token. The mechanism of passing that hash has to be a firmware ABI. Hence for any new DCS, it's necessary to add another param to that ABI.
